task.name: The concurrent gate applies a per-test bound that contention alone can reach, so load is reported as a test failure
task.story_text:
The concurrent gate enforces a five-second per-test bound. Under `-n auto --dist
worksteal` that bound is not a property of the test: it measures the test plus
scheduling delay, CPU contention, cold imports, and subprocess pressure, and then
reports the result as a test failure.

Measured on `release/v0.16`, every timeout the bound has produced was a fast test
being starved rather than a slow test misbehaving:

| test | serial | bound it crossed |
|---|---|---|
| process-group pidfile | ~1.0s | 5s |
| real-SDK import | 0.93s | 5s |
| publish timing | 1.38s | 5s |
| protected-base POC | 3.44s | **30s** |

The last row is the one that settles it: even a raised thirty-second bound was
reached, so observed inflation runs to roughly 9x. No classification of *which*
tests deserve headroom can fix that, because the variable is load, not category.

The tight threshold is also what makes it expensive, and the mechanism is not:

| configuration | suite |
|---|---|
| enforcement disabled | 123s |
| enforcement on, bound 300s | 126s |
| enforcement on, bound 5s | 156s |

Roughly 3 seconds buys per-test attribution. The remaining ~30 seconds tracks the
tight threshold rather than the mechanism; #631's implementation notes attribute
that cost to timeout-kills taking down xdist workers, which are restarted and
re-collect the whole suite — worker-restart counts were not captured in the runs
above, so that attribution is cited rather than demonstrated here.

## Why

Attribution was the point, and it works: a gate that used to die anonymously after
360 seconds now names the test and dumps its stack. That is worth keeping.

What is not working is using a tight wall-clock threshold, measured under the
suite's own parallelism, as a correctness verdict. In two days it produced an
unstable gate verdict on unchanged code (#2825), a broken baseline that refused
every sprint until cleared by hand (#2831), and a category-membership problem that
has now been re-litigated twice.

The tight bound already has a correct home. The post-stall diagnostic pass runs
serially with its own per-test bound and wall-clock cap, and exists precisely to
identify the culprit after the ordinary gate exceeds its outer budget. That is
where a tight per-test judgement measures the test rather than the machine; its
shipped default is ten seconds, under a sixty-second cap for the whole pass.

## Acceptance criteria

- The concurrent gate ships a per-test bound that the contention this suite
  actually produces cannot reach. Sixty seconds is the intended shipped value,
  against measured inflation of roughly 9x on tests of a few seconds; a smaller
  value needs evidence that inflation cannot reach it.
- No test in the default suite carries a bound above the shared one, and no
  mechanism exists to grant one: the orchestration category, its marker, and the
  module that derives membership from test source are removed rather than widened.
  Nothing is exempted, because nothing needs to be.
- Repeated runs of an unchanged commit under the gate's normal parallelism produce
  the same verdict, demonstrated across consecutive runs rather than argued.
- A test that genuinely blocks is still failed by name with a stack trace of where
  it was stuck, from the concurrent gate itself, without waiting for a later pass.
- The post-stall serial diagnostic keeps its tight per-test bound and its role
  unchanged; the tight judgement continues to be made where load is controlled.
- Every document describing the timeout contract agrees with what the suite
  enforces, and the five-second rule remains stated as the convention for an
  isolated test rather than as a gate verdict.

## Example

Today, a test measured at 1.38s serially fails the gate:

```
TIMEOUT: tests/test_sprint_run_artifact_publish_timing.py::test_repeated_terminal_publishes_leave_no_dirt_and_no_empty_commits
         exceeded its per-test bound; Exceeded its 5.0s per-test bound.
```

and passes on the next run of the same commit. Afterwards that test does not fail,
and a test that blocks indefinitely still reports as it does now — named, with the
frame it was parked on.

Supersedes #2831, which is a symptom of the classification model this removes.

conventions_soft[0].value: Coordinator is pure Python — no LLM calls for routing or process decisions

conventions_soft[1].value: Schema validation is the integrity boundary — do not relax cross-validation rules

conventions_soft[2].value: Keep modules single-purpose. Extract when a responsibility separates from its neighbours — never to satisfy a line count. Putting a change in an already-large module is correct if that is where it belongs; a module carved at whatever line got the count down is worse than the large module it came from.

conventions_soft[3].value: Keep pure-data types in low-dependency modules with stdlib-only imports

conventions_soft[4].value: Separate prompt construction, output parsing, and coordinator control flow

conventions_soft[5].value: When adding or modifying data that flows between coordinator phases, instrument the change so the actual values are visible in the audit trail — diagnosing sprint failures requires tracing real data, not reconstructing it

conventions_soft[6].value: Do not create files outside src/, tests/, or docs/. If you need a scratch file for exploration, delete it before committing.

conventions_soft[7].value: Changes that affect coordinator phase boundaries, state handoff between phases, or adaptive routing/config propagation must include seam-level integration tests covering the touched boundary. Unit tests alone are insufficient when correctness depends on cross-phase state flow.

handoff.summary: Widened the concurrent gate's shared pytest-timeout bound from 5s to 60s and deleted the raised-bound category rather than widening it. pyproject.toml now declares timeout = 60, drops the 'orchestration' marker registration, and documents the single shared bound. tests/timeout_enforcement.py lost the marker constant, the 30s ceiling, raised_bound_allowed, the orchestration_scope import, the collected-nodeid sets, and the ceiling parameter; pytest_collection_modifyitems attaches no marks at all and only rejects widening/disabling/reshaping overrides. tests/orchestration_scope.py is deleted. The four live @pytest.mark.orchestration sites were removed along with the two @pytest.mark.timeout(20) marks that existed solely to escape the 5s bound. The timeout dump hook, nodeid attribution, stack capture, and terminal-summary re-emit are unchanged, as are the serial diagnostic's 10s per-test / 60s pass defaults. CONVENTIONS.md now states five seconds as the convention for an isolated test, explains why the gate enforces 60, points the tight judgement at the post-stall serial pass, and forbids reintroducing a marker/category/list. Eleven stale 'enforced five-second per-test bound' comments across tests and src were reworded to 'convention'. The enforcement test module's classification section was replaced with the negative contract.

findings.description: The first acceptance criterion does not commit to a fixed, testable value: it says sixty seconds is 'the intended shipped value' but also permits 'a smaller value' if it comes with unspecified 'evidence.' A reviewer cannot verify pass/fail without an external judgment call on what counts as sufficient evidence, making this AC unverifiable as written.

The second acceptance criterion names implementation internals ('the orchestration category, its marker, and the module that derives membership from test source') rather than describing observable gate behavior. It should be phrased as an outcome (e.g. 'no test-level override of the per-test bound exists or can be configured') rather than requiring removal of specific named code artifacts.

soft: Coordinator is pure Python — no LLM calls for routing or process decisions
Schema validation is the integrity boundary — do not relax cross-validation rules

Keep modules single-purpose. Extract when a responsibility separates from its neighbours — never to satisfy a line count. Putting a change in an already-large module is correct if that is where it belongs; a module carved at whatever line got the count down is worse than the large module it came from.
Keep pure-data types in low-dependency modules with stdlib-only imports
Separate prompt construction, output parsing, and coordinator control flow

When adding or modifying data that flows between coordinator phases, instrument the change so the actual values are visible in the audit trail — diagnosing sprint failures requires tracing real data, not reconstructing it
Do not create files outside src/, tests/, or docs/. If you need a scratch file for exploration, delete it before committing.

Changes that affect coordinator phase boundaries, state handoff between phases, or adaptive routing/config propagation must include seam-level integration tests covering the touched boundary. Unit tests alone are insufficient when correctness depends on cross-phase state flow.

steps.description: Verify the implementation against both focused behavior and gate stability.
steps.details: After edits, run the focused timeout enforcement tests, run a blocking-test check that confirms nodeid plus stack trace attribution still comes from the concurrent gate, and run the normal parallel gate command on the same commit at least twice consecutively to demonstrate stable verdicts under `-n auto --dist worksteal`.

criteria_mapping.criterion: The concurrent gate ships a per-test bound that the contention this suite actually produces cannot reach. Sixty seconds is the intended shipped value, against measured inflation of roughly 9x on tests of a few seconds; a smaller value needs evidence that inflation cannot reach it.

No test in the default suite carries a bound above the shared one, and no mechanism exists to grant one: the orchestration category, its marker, and the module that derives membership from test source are removed rather than widened. Nothing is exempted, because nothing needs to be.
Repeated runs of an unchanged commit under the gate's normal parallelism produce the same verdict, demonstrated across consecutive runs rather than argued.
A test that genuinely blocks is still failed by name with a stack trace of where it was stuck, from the concurrent gate itself, without waiting for a later pass.
The post-stall serial diagnostic keeps its tight per-test bound and its role unchanged; the tight judgement continues to be made where load is controlled.
Every document describing the timeout contract agrees with what the suite enforces, and the five-second rule remains stated as the convention for an isolated test rather than as a gate verdict.
